The Revenger's Tragedy. This visceral Jacobean revenge play, attributed variously to Thomas Middleton or Cyril Tourneur with the question still unresolved, descends into a riot of poisoning, assassination, and cannibalistic revenge where nearly every character is both predator and prey.

Vindice holds the skull of his slain beloved, Gloriana. Driven by this relic and by rage at the Duke's libertine cruelty, he orchestrates an elaborate revenge spanning two acts. The Duke, a senile voluptuary, attempts to seduce Castiza, Vindice's virtuous sister. Vindice's mother Gratiana initially encourages the seduction for money, then repents, creating a plot of familial betrayal and redemption.

Vindice poisons the skull with toxin and places it in the Duke's path. When the Duke kisses it, mistaking it for a living woman, he absorbs the venom and dies in agony. The revenge then cascades outward. Vindice kills the Duke's son Lussurioso in a brothel. The Duchess and her illegitimate children are poisoned by a banquet. Murder begets murder in exponential chaos.

Spurio, the Duchess's bastard, and the Duke's legitimate heirs vie for dominance. All are morally compromised, and the revenge becomes indiscriminate destruction of the entire court. Yet Vindice's final revelation of his own hand in the murders, his confession driven by pride, leads to his own execution. Revenge consumes the avenger.

The play's language is densely metaphorical and grotesque, filled with disease imagery, sexual transgression, and skull rhetoric—a verbal and visual feast of corruption and decay. Whether written by Middleton or Tourneur, this is the revenge tragedy's darkest and most nihilistic expression, revenge itself portrayed as a disease consuming all who touch it.
